lesson.title: The Size of the Pipe: What Bandwidth Actually Measures
lesson.summary: Bandwidth is the maximum rate at which a communication link can carry data, a ceiling set by the physical medium and equipment rather than a guarantee of what any particular transfer will actually achieve.
lesson.body:
Every communication link, whether it is a fiber optic cable, a copper Ethernet cable, or a wireless radio channel, has some upper limit on how fast it can physically carry data. Bandwidth is the name for that limit, expressed in bits per second and scaled up to kilobits, megabits, or gigabits per second for the speeds involved in modern networks. It is a property of the link itself: its physical medium, its signaling technology, and the equipment on each end all set an upper bound on how many bits per second can be pushed through, independent of whatever traffic happens to be using it at any given moment.

The term has an older, more literal meaning worth knowing, because it explains where the word came from. In electrical engineering, bandwidth originally referred to a range of frequencies, measured in Hertz, that a channel could carry. Claude Shannon's channel capacity theorem showed that a channel's maximum achievable data rate in bits per second grows with both its bandwidth in Hertz and its signal-to-noise ratio, which is precisely why the word bandwidth drifted from meaning a range of frequencies to meaning, colloquially in networking, a maximum data rate. Both usages describe the same underlying idea: how much capacity a physical channel offers.

A useful analogy is a water pipe. The pipe's diameter sets a hard ceiling on how much water could possibly flow through it per second under ideal conditions, but the actual flow at any moment depends on water pressure, whether a valve is partly closed, and whether other pipes are drawing from the same source. Bandwidth is the diameter, fixed by construction. It is not a promise about what any specific transfer will experience, only a ceiling on what is physically possible.

Internet service plans make this concrete. An ISP advertising a 100 Mbps home internet plan is stating the bandwidth of the link connecting that home to the ISP's network, the maximum rate that link's physical medium and equipment can support. That number does not mean a given file download will move at 100 Mbps, because the download's actual observed speed depends on far more than the link's raw capacity, including congestion elsewhere on the path, the capabilities of the sending server, and the behavior of the transport protocol carrying the data. That distinction between the ceiling and the observed reality is exactly the gap the next concept, throughput, is built to describe.

A common source of confusion is worth clearing up here: bandwidth is conventionally expressed in bits per second, using a lowercase b, while file sizes on a computer are conventionally expressed in bytes, using an uppercase B, and there are eight bits in a byte. A 100 Mbps connection therefore transfers at most about 12.5 megabytes per second, not 100 megabytes per second, which is a common point of disappointment when someone compares an advertised connection speed against the download speed reported by their operating system. Getting this conversion right is a small but genuinely useful piece of literacy for reasoning about any communication link's real capacity.
